title: How to Ask for a Raise Without Another Job Offer: 3 Scripts
meta_description: Learn how to ask for a raise without another job offer: build an evidence file, check market pay, time your ask and use 3 word-for-word scripts.
quick_answer: To ask for a raise without another job offer, make your case with evidence instead of leverage. Document your results and how your role has grown. Research market pay for your role and location, and ask before budgets are set. Request a specific figure in a dedicated meeting. If the answer is 'not now', agree a dated review or non-cash items in writing.
key_takeaways: You don't need leverage to ask for a raise. A one- or two-page evidence file covering your results, how your role has grown and the skills you've added gives your manager something to take to whoever approves budgets.
Base your number on market data you've checked yourself for your role, level and location. Don't base it on your expenses or on what a colleague earns.
Raise the topic before pay budgets are locked, which often happens weeks or months before formal reviews. Don't bring up money for the first time in the review meeting itself.
Ask for one specific figure, then stop talking and let your manager answer.
If the answer is 'not now', leave with a review date, measurable criteria and a written summary, or with a non-cash win you actually want.
No approach guarantees a yes. Even a clear no is useful information for your next career decision.
who_this_is_for: This guide is for salaried employees who think they're underpaid, don't have a competing offer (or don't want to bluff about one), and want a calm, evidence-based way to ask their manager for more.
intro: Most raise advice assumes you have leverage, usually another job offer. But plenty of people like their job, aren't job hunting and don't want to claim an offer they don't have. You can still make a strong case. This guide shows you how to build an evidence file, check market pay for your role and location, and time the conversation around your employer's budget cycle. You'll get three word-for-word scripts: one for the opening ask, one for pushback and one for a 'not now' answer. You'll also find a follow-up email template and a list of things to negotiate when money genuinely isn't available. One honest caveat: no script guarantees a yes. Good preparation improves your odds and means you leave with something, whether that's more money, a dated plan or a clear picture of where you stand.

steps.name: Build your evidence file
steps.text: Start from the date your pay was last set and list your results, how your role has grown, any new skills and any recognition. Write one line per item using the pattern action → result → why it mattered. Put a three-sentence summary at the top.

steps.name: Research your market range
steps.text: Collect at least three data points for your role, level and location. Good sources are government wage data, salary-sharing sites, professional association surveys and job postings that list pay. Write down where each figure came from and when you found it.

steps.name: Set your ask and your floor
steps.text: Choose one specific figure you can back up with your evidence file and market data. Also decide on a private minimum you'd consider fair, and don't share it.

steps.name: Time it around the budget cycle
steps.text: Ask your manager or HR when pay budgets and review decisions are set, and whether pay can be adjusted outside the normal review cycle. Raise the topic before budgets are locked.

steps.name: Book a dedicated meeting
steps.text: Ask for 30 minutes in person or on video with a neutral title such as 'Compensation conversation'. For example: 'I'd like to talk about my role and compensation. Could we find 30 minutes in the next two weeks?'

steps.name: Make the ask and pause
steps.text: Use the opening script to summarise your case, cite your market research and state one specific figure. Then stop talking and let your manager respond, even if the silence feels long.

steps.name: Handle pushback with evidence
steps.text: Give your strongest example of how your role has grown. Then ask what figure your manager could support and what you'd need to show to close the gap.

steps.name: Turn 'not now' into a plan
steps.text: Agree a specific review date, measurable criteria and a target figure. Ask about non-cash options too, such as a new title, a training budget or more flexibility.

steps.name: Confirm in writing
steps.text: Within a day, email a short summary of what was agreed. Add the review date to your calendar, with a reminder two weeks before it.

sections.heading: Why you don't need a competing offer to ask for a raise
paragraphs: You don't need a competing offer to ask for a raise. You need a clear, documented case that your pay no longer matches the value and scope of your work. An outside offer is only one kind of leverage, and bluffing about one is risky. Your manager may ask for details, see through it or simply tell you to take it.

An evidence-based ask works differently because it gives your manager something to use instead of pressure. In many organisations, managers can't approve raises alone. They often have to justify an above-standard or off-cycle increase to HR, finance or their own boss, and a clear one-page case makes that easier.

Good preparation improves your odds, but it can't guarantee a yes. Budgets, company performance and internal pay bands can block a raise even when your case is strong. Aim to leave the conversation with one of three things: more money, a specific plan with a date, or clear information about where you stand.
bullets: No credibility risk: everything you say can be checked, and it holds up when it is.
Reusable: the same evidence file supports reviews, promotion cases and future job searches.
Informative: even a no tells you whether growth is realistic where you are.

sections.heading: How to build an evidence file your manager can forward
paragraphs: An evidence file is a short document, ideally one or two pages, that lists your results, how your role has grown and the skills you've added since your pay was last set. Write it as if your manager will paste it straight into an approval request, because they might.

Start from the date of your last pay change, not just the last 12 months. Go through your calendar, sent email, project tracker, past reviews and any messages praising your work. Sort what you find into four groups: results, scope growth, skills added and recognition.

Write each item as one line using the pattern action → result → why it mattered. For example: 'Rebuilt the monthly reporting process → cut preparation from three days to one → finance now closes the month earlier.' Use your own figures and label estimates as estimates, so nothing falls apart if someone asks.

If your work is hard to measure, use counts, before-and-after comparisons and signs of quality instead of revenue. Examples include tickets resolved, new hires trained, processes documented, errors caught before release, and tasks that now run without your manager's involvement.
Put a three-sentence summary at the top: what you're asking for, why, and what you'll keep delivering. Keep confidential company data out of personal apps unless your employer's policy allows it.
bullets: Results: outcomes with real numbers where possible, such as revenue influenced, costs cut, hours saved, errors reduced, customers retained or deadlines met.
Scope growth: responsibilities you've added, people you now train or supervise, bigger clients or budgets, and work you took over when a colleague left.
Skills added: certifications, tools or capabilities the team now relies on you for.
Recognition: specific feedback from clients, peers or leaders, quoted accurately and dated.

sections.heading: How to research market pay for your role and location
paragraphs: To research market pay, collect several independent data points for your role, level and location, then turn them into a range. Don't go looking for one 'correct' number.

Useful sources include government wage statistics, salary-sharing websites, pay surveys from professional associations and recruiters who specialise in your field. In the US, the Bureau of Labor Statistics publishes occupational wage data by area, and national statistics offices in many other countries run similar surveys. Every source has blind spots. Government data can lag and uses broad job categories, and crowdsourced sites only reflect people who chose to report.

Job postings are often the most current signal. Some states, cities and countries now require employers to publish pay ranges in job ads. Search for roles that match what you actually do and record the ranges you find. The rules vary, so check what applies where you live and work.

Then set two numbers. Your ask is a specific figure you can justify with both market data and your evidence file, usually in the upper part of your researched range. Your floor is the lowest outcome you'd consider fair. You say your ask out loud. Your floor stays private.
bullets: Match roles on responsibilities and seniority, not job title alone.
Use pay data for your location, or your employer's stated pay policy if you work remotely.
Record the source and date of every data point so you can explain where it came from.
Keep base salary separate from bonus, equity and benefits.
Leave out outliers you can't explain.
Ask HR whether your company has a pay band for your level, and where you currently sit in it.

sections.heading: When to ask for a raise: budget cycles, reviews and bad timing
paragraphs: The best time to ask is usually before your company sets its pay budget. Once budgets are locked, even a supportive manager has little room to move.

Many employers decide merit increases weeks or months before formal reviews, and the financial year doesn't always start in January. Ask your manager or HR three simple questions: When are pay and promotion budgets set? When are review decisions made? Can pay be adjusted outside the normal review cycle?
Within that cycle, the strongest moments are usually just before budget planning or soon after a visible win. The riskiest are during layoffs, hiring freezes or a crisis your manager is handling.

If you're unsure about timing, raise it early with a low-pressure message: 'I'd like to talk about my compensation ahead of this year's review cycle. When would be a good time?' This gives your manager time to prepare and shows you understand how decisions get made.
bullets: Good timing: just before budget planning, shortly after a visible win, after you've formally taken on new responsibilities, or after a strong review.
Riskier timing: during layoffs or hiring freezes, right after weak company results, while your manager is dealing with a crisis, or in a passing hallway or chat conversation.
Avoid bringing up money for the first time in the review meeting itself. By then the numbers have often already been decided.

sections.heading: How to ask for a raise without another job offer: word-for-word scripts
paragraphs: The three scripts below give you exact wording for the moments that matter most: the opening ask, pushback and a 'not now' answer. They help you stay calm and specific without mentioning other offers.

Book a dedicated meeting in person or on video, not by email alone, and bring your evidence file. Practise the scripts aloud a few times and adjust the wording so it sounds like you. Prepare short answers to three likely questions: 'Where does that number come from?', 'Why now?' and 'Are you looking elsewhere?'

Script 1, the opening ask: “Thanks for making time for this. I'd like to talk about my pay. Since my salary was last set in [month/year], my role has grown: I've [result with number], [second result], and I've taken on [new responsibility]. I've also researched market pay for [role] at my level in [location], and similar roles are advertising roughly [range]. Based on that, I'm asking for an increase to [specific figure]. I've put the details on one page and can send it to you after this.” Then stop talking and let your manager respond, even if the silence feels long.

Script 2, for pushback such as “That's more than we usually give” or “Everyone gets the standard increase”: “I understand there's a standard increase, and I appreciate it. My request is different because the job I'm doing now is bigger than the one I was hired for. For example, [your strongest example]. I'm asking whether my pay can match the role I'm actually doing. If [figure] isn't possible, what could you support, and what would I need to show to close the gap?”

Script 3, for a 'not now' answer such as “There's no budget” or “Let's revisit later”: “Thanks for being straight with me. Can we agree on what 'later' means? I'd suggest we set a date, say [specific month], and agree now on the results that would justify [figure] by then. Would you be willing to confirm that in a short email? In the meantime, is there flexibility on anything else, such as [title, training budget or schedule]?”
bullets: Ask for a specific number, not 'a bit more' or a vague range.
Make the case about your value and market pay, not your personal expenses.
Don't bring up colleagues' salaries, because it pulls the conversation away from your own work.
Don't apologise for asking or over-explain. One or two strong examples beat a long list.
If you're asked whether you're looking elsewhere and you aren't, say so: “I'm not actively looking. I'd like to grow here, which is why I'm raising this directly.”
Don't threaten to leave unless you're genuinely ready to.

sections.heading: What to negotiate when money is off the table
paragraphs: If a raise genuinely isn't possible right now, negotiate a dated plan to revisit pay, non-cash items that matter to you, or both. Get the agreement in writing.

The dated plan matters most, because vague promises like 'we'll look at it next year' are easy to forget, especially if your manager changes jobs. A solid plan has a specific date, measurable criteria, a target figure and a written record you both keep.

Non-cash items can be easier to approve because they may come from other budgets or need only your manager's sign-off. The comparison table in this guide sets out the common options and their catches. Pick things that help your career or daily life, not consolation prizes you don't want.

Be careful with a title change on its own. A stronger title can raise your future market value, but it can also mean more responsibility for the same pay. If you accept one, pair it with a dated pay review.
bullets: A specific review date, not a season or quarter.
Measurable criteria you'll meet by that date.
The target figure or range you're working toward.
Who else needs to approve it, and whether your manager will raise it with them in advance.
A written summary you both keep.

sections.heading: What to do after the conversation, whatever the answer
paragraphs: Within a day, send a short email confirming what was agreed. Then deliver your side of the plan, which makes the next conversation easier.

Follow-up email template: “Hi [Name], thanks for today's conversation. To confirm what we discussed: [outcome, for example: you'll take a request for [figure] to [approver] by [date], or we'll revisit on [date] once I've delivered [criteria]]. I'll keep you updated on progress. Let me know if I've missed anything.”

If the answer is yes, confirm the new figure, the date it takes effect and when it will appear in your pay, then check your first payslip. If you agreed a plan instead, add the review date to your calendar, update your evidence file monthly and remind your manager about two weeks before the date.

If the answer is a clear no with no path forward, treat it as information, not failure. Ask what growth realistically looks like in your role, then take a few days before you decide anything. You might stay for the experience, flexibility or stability. Or you might start looking at other roles, and any offer you get then will be real, not a bluff.

faq.question: Can you ask for a raise without a competing job offer?
faq.answer: Yes. Raises are commonly granted for strong performance, bigger responsibilities and pay that has fallen behind the market, not only because of outside offers. A documented case gives your manager something concrete to take to the people who approve budgets, and it avoids the risks of bluffing.

faq.question: How much of a raise should I ask for?
faq.answer: No single percentage fits every role or company. Base your number on market data you've checked for your role, level and location, plus how much your responsibilities have grown. Ask for a specific figure you can justify, usually in the upper part of your researched range, and keep a private minimum in mind.

faq.question: What should I say if my manager says there's no budget for a raise?
faq.answer: Ask when the budget will next be reviewed, then agree a specific date, measurable criteria and a target figure for revisiting your pay. In the meantime, ask whether non-cash options such as a title change, training budget or more flexibility are possible. Confirm everything in a follow-up email.

faq.question: Should I ask for a raise by email or in person?
faq.answer: Make the ask in a live conversation, in person or on video, so you can talk it through and answer questions as they come up. Use email to request the meeting beforehand and to confirm in writing what was agreed afterwards.

faq.question: Is it OK to ask for a raise outside of review season?
faq.answer: Yes, especially if your role has changed a lot, but a raise outside the normal review cycle may need extra approval. Ask your manager or HR whether that's possible at your company. If it isn't, find out when the next budget decisions are made and raise the topic before then.

faq.question: What should I do if my raise request is turned down?
faq.answer: Ask what would need to change for the answer to be yes, and ask for that plan in writing. If there's no realistic path, take a few days to decide whether to stay, focus on non-cash growth or look at other roles. Any outside offer you get after that will be genuine rather than a bluff.

conclusion: To ask for a raise without another job offer, replace leverage with evidence. Document what you've delivered and how your role has grown, check market pay for your own role and location, and raise the topic before budgets are locked. Then ask for a specific number in a calm, dedicated conversation. If the answer is yes, confirm it in writing. If it's 'not now', leave with a date, clear criteria and a written record, or with a non-cash win that genuinely helps you. If it's a firm no, you'll still have a clear answer and an up-to-date evidence file, which puts you in a strong position to decide your next career move.
